o: We must apply exactly one range-add of some value x to some contiguous subarray, then report the maximum frequency of k. Elements equal to v inside the chosen window become k (when x = k - v), but elements already equal to k inside the window are destroyed. So for each candidate source value v != k, we want a window maximizing (#v - #k) inside it; the final frequency is base_count(k) plus that surplus. If no window helps, the answer is just the original count of k. In Example 2, v = 2 with x = 8 over the whole tail yields 4 twos converted against 0 existing tens. Values are bounded by 50, so trying all v is cheap.
k: Only x = k - v for some existing value v matters; any other x cannot create new k's.
For fixed v, best gain of a window = max over windows of (count_v - count_k), found by a simple sliding window that shrinks whenever count_k exceeds count_v.
Answer = max(base frequency of k, base frequency + best gain over all v).

a.i: Since nums[i] <= 50, iterate each candidate v in 1..50 (skip v = k). Maintain a window where we track cv = count of v and ck = count of k; a window is only useful while cv > ck, so shrink from the left whenever ck >= cv, and record cv - ck as the best surplus.
s: For each v != k, slide a window keeping cv > ck, tracking max(cv - ck).
Return base + overall best surplus (or base if no surplus).
a.t: O(50n) — one linear pass per candidate value

w: Pick this approach directly; the small value bound is the intended lever. Pitfall: forgetting that k's inside the window are destroyed (that is why the window condition is ck < cv), and remembering the operation must happen but may be a no-op window (covered by returning base alone). Follow-up: what if values were unbounded? You would need coordinate compression or a map keyed by value.
